title: Google's SynthID watermark is hard to break, but it doesn't solve AI misinformation
gist: Hands-on testing found Google's SynthID watermark survived 300 generations of compression, resizing and screenshotting, but a 20 percent crop after heavy compression removed it entirely. The deeper argument is that watermarking cannot solve AI misinformation because open models produce unlabeled content, detectors are fragmented and rate-limited to about 10 checks a day, and the scarce asset is cryptographically provenanced real content via C2PA.

insights.claim: Starling Lab estimates it took until 1975, 149 years after the camera's invention, for humanity to create 1.5 billion images, while generative AI produced the same volume in just 18 months.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: The supply curve for imagery has broken; any business model priced on image scarcity is being repriced.
insights.quote: it took until 1975—149 years after the invention of the camera—for humanity to create 1.5 billion images. It took generative AI just 18 months to do the same.
insights.locator: The scale of AI-generated media

insights.claim: Google announced at I/O that its tools alone had been used to create more than 100 billion AI images and videos in a couple of years, and Google is far from the only source.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: 100 billion assets from one vendor sets the floor for how much content any labeling regime must cover.
insights.locator: This spring, Google announced at I/O

insights.claim: The author asserts AI content has already eclipsed authentic content on the Internet, making comprehensive labeling of AI output structurally impossible.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: If synthetic already outweighs authentic, verification of the real becomes the tractable problem and labeling the fake does not.
insights.locator: The scale of AI content alone will make it impossible to label all of it.

insights.claim: SynthID survived 300 simulated sharing generations of random compression and resizing on both a fully AI-generated image and an AI-edited photo, and also survives screenshotting because the watermark pixels transfer to the new file.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: The watermark is genuinely durable to incidental degradation, so casual laundering of AI images will not defeat it.
insights.locator: And look at that—the SynthID watermark still works

insights.claim: The failure mode is cropping combined with compression: after 300 compression generations a 20 percent border crop rendered SynthID undetectable, and a 50 percent crop broke it around 250 iterations.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: The removal recipe is trivially available to any motivated actor, so watermark presence is a weak evidentiary signal.
insights.quote: These versions (see below) have been cropped by 20 percent, but that’s enough to render SynthID undetectable.
insights.locator: This is where we finally find the limits of SynthID

insights.claim: Meta's recently released Content Seal AI watermark is far weaker, with Reuters finding that simply cropping images would often eliminate it, showing watermark robustness varies enormously between vendors.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Do not treat 'watermarked' as a uniform property; per-vendor robustness testing is required before relying on any label.
insights.locator: Meta released its Content Seal AI watermark recently

insights.claim: Google's own original SynthID paper states the watermark is not intended to withstand adversarial attacks, and DeepMind's Pushmeet Kohli says only that the team designed against transformations like filters and cropping.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: The vendor has already disclaimed the threat model that matters most for disinformation, which caps how much weight regulators should place on it.
insights.quote: Through the whole development process, we sort of assumed that a technology like this will be attacked
insights.locator: Google also doesn’t claim that SynthID is invulnerable

insights.claim: With OpenAI, Runway and Nvidia adopting SynthID, most of the consumer AI space now depends on one watermarking technology, which makes it a single high-value target whose compromise could unlabel billions of assets at once.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Standard concentration creates correlated failure risk in the entire AI-provenance stack; monitor for a credible SynthID break.
insights.quote: all those billions of AI images and videos could be unlabeled in a snap
insights.locator: Still, security is never perfect

insights.claim: Google deliberately withholds SynthID mitigation details and provides no public API or detector webpage, requiring users to ask Gemini to run the verifier, an explicit security-through-restricted-access model.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Restricted verification means third parties, including newsrooms and platforms, cannot build automated provenance pipelines on SynthID.
insights.locator: Google doesn’t want to give people an easy path to attack SynthID

insights.claim: Google limits SynthID to approximately 10 image checks per day and locks users out faster if they upload too many similar images, so verification comes with a cooldown period during active disinformation events.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Rate limiting makes SynthID useless for at-scale content moderation, which is where the actual demand sits.
insights.quote: Google limits SynthID to “approximately 10 image checks” per day
insights.locator: To prevent people from using successive AI checks

insights.claim: Watermarks are fragmenting even among SynthID adopters: Google's detector does not recognize OpenAI's watermark and OpenAI's detector does not recognize Google's, so a negative check proves nothing.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Detector fragmentation guarantees false negatives; any policy requiring platforms to detect AI content is currently unimplementable.
insights.quote: Google’s detector doesn’t recognize OpenAI’s watermark, and OpenAI’s detector doesn’t recognize Google’s watermark.
insights.locator: As Google rolls out the technology to other firms

insights.claim: A Google spokesperson concedes the fragmented verification experience is suboptimal and offers only a vague vision of a more interoperable ecosystem with industry partners.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: No committed timeline for interoperability means the fragmentation problem persists through at least the next election cycle.
insights.locator: A Google spokesperson says the team is aware

insights.claim: Watermarking can never be sufficient because there will always be ways to create AI content without any labeling, and countless generation companies are unlikely to all adopt watermarks or metadata.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Any regulatory or product strategy premised on universal AI labeling is built on an assumption that cannot hold.
insights.locator: Watermarks in AI will never be the best way

insights.claim: Starling Lab fellow Adam Rose argues the real problem is not content from Google and OpenAI but people running their own models locally, where open models generate images with no labeling whatsoever and can be shared and improved indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Open-weight local generation is the uncontrollable tail; enforcement leverage exists only over centralized providers.
insights.quote: The problem is people who can run their own models, who can do things on their own computers.
insights.locator: I think the bigger problem here is not just the images

insights.claim: As labeling becomes more common, people may wrongly assume that unlabeled images and videos are automatically legitimate, a dangerous inference that makes partial watermark coverage actively misleading.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Partial labeling creates a false-authenticity halo, meaning incomplete watermark rollouts can worsen the misinformation problem.
insights.locator: Since there will always be unlabeled AI content

insights.claim: Adam Rose frames the shift in supply-and-demand terms: unlimited content supply crashes the value of content while creating growing demand for authenticated content that can be proven to be what it purports to be.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: The investable thesis is provenance infrastructure and verified-content marketplaces, not AI detection tools.
insights.quote: It’s economics 101, supply and demand. Supply goes through the roof, and the value of content is going to continue to crash.
insights.locator: The future that we live in will increasingly be a world of unlimited content

insights.claim: Photojournalist and Starling fellow Mike Caronna argues that because physical-camera content is inherently limited while synthetic content is not, the strategic pivot should be to secure and prove the authenticity of scarce truthful information.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Camera-captured, cryptographically signed media becomes a differentiated asset class for news organizations and archives.
insights.quote: That’s why we want to pivot to what’s scarce, and what’s scarce is high-value, truthful information.
insights.locator: There’s a limit to how much content can be created

insights.claim: The liar's dividend, where public figures dismiss real evidence of wrongdoing as AI-generated fakery, is identified as the concrete harm that provenance systems must defend against.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Deniability of real evidence, not fake evidence itself, is the accountability risk that drives institutional demand for provenance.
insights.locator: The liar’s dividend is a rhetorical strategy

insights.claim: C2PA metadata is cryptographically secure and cannot be faked, but it is trivially easy to strip because simply editing and saving an image or taking a screenshot removes it, which is why Google pairs it with SynthID.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: The two technologies have opposite failure modes, so neither alone is deployable; combined systems are the only viable design.
insights.quote: Simply editing and saving an image or taking a screenshot can remove C2PA.
insights.locator: There are currently two approaches to labeling AI content

insights.claim: Google's Pixel phones are the only mainstream cameras with deep C2PA integration, with Pixel 10 images and videos carrying cryptographically protected metadata on when and how they were captured and whether AI altered them.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: A concrete hardware differentiator for Google and a gap for Apple and Samsung; watch for competitive C2PA adoption in phones.
insights.quote: The company’s Pixel phones are the only mainstream cameras with deep C2PA integration.
insights.locator: The problem is that C2PA is still rare

insights.claim: The author's conclusion is that verifying what is real, rather than outing what is fake, is the more tractable strategy, and that labeling AI content is good policy for tech firms but will not solve misinformation.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Directs capital and policy attention toward provenance and tamper-evident capture rather than AI detectors.
insights.quote: Labeling AI content is a good policy for tech firms, but it won’t save us.
insights.locator: In the future, we may have no choice
